opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we first launched Meshy publicly, I didn't trust any single number to tell me whether the quality was good. In 3D generation the academic metrics, things like Chamfer distance or various CLIP-based scores, don't really capture what a user cares about. A model can score well and still give you a mesh that's unusable in a game engine because the topology is a mess or the textures are blurry from one side.

So I judged it in a very practical way. First, I used it myself, a lot. Every day I'd generate dozens of assets and ask: would I actually put this in a project? Would a game developer or a 3D artist accept this as a starting point, or would they throw it away and start from scratch? That "would you keep it" test was much more honest than any benchmark.

Second, we watched user behavior very closely. Do people download the model, or do they generate and leave? Do they come back the next day? Do they regenerate the same prompt five times because the first four were bad? Those signals tell you about quality in a way that's hard to fake.

Third, we listened to the community. When you launch publicly, people are not polite. They'll post the weird results, the three-legged chairs, the faces that look melted. That was painful but super valuable, because it showed us the failure modes we hadn't seen internally.

And to be honest, at launch the quality was far from perfect. But my view was that it only needed to be good enough that some group of people found it genuinely useful, saving them real time. If that's true, you can iterate quickly. If you wait until it's perfect, you'll never ship, and you'll also miss the feedback you need to get there.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes practical quality checks, user behavior, and community feedback, but does not say Yuanming Hu asked interview participants to conceal that he created Mesh.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't trust my own judgment at that point, so I tried not to judge it myself at all. When you've been staring at something for months, you lose the ability to see it the way a new user does. So the launch was really about collecting signal from people who had no context.

I looked at a few things. The first was whether people got to a result they were happy with without asking me anything. If someone had to come to Discord and ask "how do I do X," that was a quality failure on our side, not theirs. The second was retention, not signups. Signups on launch day are mostly curiosity. What I cared about was whether the same person came back on day three or day seven and generated something new. That's a much more honest number.

And then there was a softer thing, which was watching what people made. If the outputs people shared looked like our demo examples, that meant the product was only good along the path we had tuned. If they made things we never anticipated, that told me the model and the tooling actually generalized, which is the real bar.

I'll admit the early version was rough. There were plenty of cases where the geometry was off or the texture didn't line up, and we saw every one of those in public. But I'd rather launch with a clear picture of what's broken than polish in private based on my own taste. The users ended up setting the quality bar for us, and that was the point.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from public users, retention, and shared outputs, but does not say Yuanming Hu asked prospective interview participants to keep his role in creating Mesh secret.

astra-6.text: For me, the key question was whether people could actually use what Mesh generated. A model can look impressive in a demo, but the real test is what happens when someone brings their own idea and tries to use the result. So I’d judge quality by how closely it matched their intent, how much cleanup it needed, and whether it saved them time. Visual quality matters, but usefulness is the stronger signal.

r001.rationale: The response discusses judging Mesh by usefulness, intent match, cleanup, and time saved. It does not report that Hu asked interview participants to keep his authorship of Mesh confidential.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the key question was whether people could actually use what it generated. A result can look impressive at first glance, but that’s different from being useful. So I’d judge the quality by looking at the outputs and listening to users: did it give them something they wanted, and how much work did they still have to do? I wouldn’t call it good just because we had launched it publicly.
